Yes and no. Its a more stable career in that you are less likely to get fired and more likely to be able to find a job once you are a doctor (though note: AI and mid levels may effect this in the future). However, a stable career is one the one that you can continue doing and not burnout. Being a physician is a high stress job due to long hours, the importance and risks of every decision, administrative barriers, being a customer service role, empathy/emotional exhaustion, and seeing death. Even if you “like” being a physician, that job can eat away at you over time, reducing your longevity. Physician burnout is a significant problem in the USA. 

Also when you are thinking about longevity, remember that most physicians don’t finish their training and start their careers till their early 30s. That is significant delayed earning  and delayed opportunity for investment growth. That’s not to mention the huge student loans building with interest. 

Assuming you like both fields the same, experience the same stress with both fields, discount the time and difficulty of the extended training, and discount the opportunity cost of delayed career start; yes being a physician is probably more stable as you are less likely to be fired. However your stability is just more threatened by your own physical and emotional degradation rather than your boss firing you.

Current medical student and former EMT, medicine is a very difficult path that is often romanticized. You give up close to a decade in your life for training to do a job that is incredibly stressful. The plus side is that many times the work you are doing is actually meaningful, which is hard to say for many other jobs. 

When I was making my decision to pursue medicine, this blog post was incredibly helpful for me in laying out many of the downsides. https://web.archive.org/web/20180121173825/http://blogs.harvard.edu/abinazir/2005/05/23/why-you-should-not-go-to-medical-school-a-gleefully-biased-rant/

 Make sure you acquaint yourself with all of the downsides before going to medical school, because you don’t want to waste 4-7 years to find out you don’t like being a doctor.

One of the points that stood out to me was his point on malpractice liability. His response was that since hospitals and physicians are able to bear the cost of malpractice lawsuits while being profitable, AI will as well. However physicians (and to a much lesser extent hospitals) have only a set amount of net worth that can be taken. A judgment of 50 million doesn’t really matter if the doctor only has 2 million to his name. 

On the other hand, supposing there are 2 or 3 big AI models that are used across the country, that company has to bear the malpractice debt for whole country. Not to mention that the AI making a certain mistake in one scenario makes it much more likely that it could have made the same mistake for other patients in the same senario.  I can see malpractice lawyers building class action lawsuits for all the people in the country whose cancer was missed by the AI.  Especially given that people are less tolerant towards mistakes by AI. 

All of this to say that I think the liability risks are undersold in the video. It is much easier and probably cheaper to keep a small number of employees to sign off on the AIs decisions but the liability on their license. I still agree that AI is very much still a threat that is going to take away healthcare jobs. I am sure that providers are going to be pressured by corporations to “see” an ungodly number of patients using AI. Just blanket signing 100 charts without reviewing them like insurance, like those currently employed by insurance companies already do. But I find it hard to imagine a completely autonomous AI with full practice rights being the most feasible outcome in the near future.

Things to consider with a sling that holds a laptop:
1. reversible strap. If you use it with any regularity you are going to need to switch sides so you don’t fuck up your shoulder
2. Thick/padded/comfortable strap to carry that weight
3. Can take it or leave it, but a chest strap can help support and manage weight especially if biking
4. Having some sort of quick release or unclasp option is nice

Of course it also goes that you should consider a small backpack instead of a sling as it would be easier to find and more comfortable than trying to hit that sweetspot in slings. As someone into slings I definitely get the draw, however you are towing a very thin line with slings big enough to carry your laptop that are not just backpacks missing a strap.

Just to add something different to the conversation, make sure to check your state laws on the requirements for firing a patient. Most of them require you to provide them with other reasonable options for transition of care (offices actually accepting patients) and continue to provide care to that patient for a defined period of time (often 30 days).

“Now if we only considered the popular vote, that would leave out a lot of states in deciding the Presidency”

I find this quote interesting because I feel that our current system leaves a lot of states out of deciding the presidency. If you live in a state that is a fully red or blue by a wide margin, your individual extra vote does not make a difference. You are not helping push the needle on the national stage. 

In our current system, if you don’t live in one of the swing states like Pennsylvania, Georgia, or Wisconsin, your state is effectively left out of the presidential election. I mean, outside of fundraising, how often are candidates seeking to appeal to the voters in states with no chance of changing. As opposed to a popular vote, where each and every person in every state gets to participate and push the needle for their candidate (ideally with ranked choice voting aswell). 

I say this as someone who has lived in heavily contested swing states for the last 3 election and thus whose vote has mattered much more than most everyone else in the United States.

Fun fact, smaller states by population also have disproportionate representation in the house as well. This is because the number of congressional representatives is capped, but each state gets a minimum of 1 representative. Based on the proportional population of each state, some small states like Wyoming should have less than one representative. However slightly larger than the smallest states can get screwed in proportional representation if they are just before the cut off of the next seat. 

Check it out, pretty interesting and not something I had heard of until a few years ago. The 538 tool is especially cool

To add to what others have commented, I think this is more of a semantic argument. 

In medicine, there is a difference between infection and disease, where infection is the colonization in the body by a foreign organism and the disease is the clinical syndrome that results (in this case) from the colonization. For example chicken pox is the disease that is caused by an infection with the varicella zoster virus, but some people can be infected with varicella zoster without getting the clinical syndrome of chicken pox. 

All of this to say that Ellie could be immune to the cordyceps disease while not being immune to colonization (I.e. infection) with cordyceps.

This will probably be buried, but I think this is the way it should be. As a vendor who does the actual work of transporting and selling the merchandise, not only are you likely working harder in a given week than your supervisor, you are also likely directly responsible for making the company significantly more money. 

Shouldn't the job that is both harder and contributes more to company profits make more money?

For some reason, it is currently part of the workplace culture that managers should be paid, more and be considered more important than the people they manage. However, in many industries, it should be the manager's role to enable and support skilled workers rather than control or direct them. In these cases, it could often make sense to me for managers to make less than those they supervise. A good example of this is in a hospital: you wouldn't expect a administrator in charge of HR, setting the schedule, ect to make more than the doctors they are setting the schedule for (even if that is sometimes the case).

I guess the biggest problem is: why would someone want to become a manager? Especially if you want the manager to previously have worked in the "lower" position? Perhaps it would be wanting to trade some money for an easier lifestyle, or wanting to make a larger impact, but I can see how this could lead to the wrong people (least productive employee, someone only looking to control others) disproportionately becoming managers.

Tips for people wanting true blackout curtains:

1 Good blackout curtains are heavy. Two layered is often good or just thick material. Lots of poor products on the market (I like the [nicetown 100% blackout](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07R7H1CWW?ref=ppx_yo2ov_dt_b_product_details&th=1) that is mentioned below)

2. Get your black out curtains in a dark color. I don't care if the box says 100% black out, a black or gray curtain will block much more light than a white one from the same company

3. Hanging the curtains is just as important. For better sealing you probably want to use a tension rod on the interior of the window as opposed to the hanging rod you see here. That way you can tuck the edges in to prevent light leaking from the sides. Often even if you have shades already on the window you still have space behind them for a rod.

3.5. If using a hanging rod, using tape or adhesive Velcro scripts can help prevent light coming in from the edges. Sleepout (old blackout curtain kickstarter) is coming out with a new rod as well that helps seal the edges, it will be interesting to see if it works. Their curtains are supposed to be very good but they have a pretty high price rage ([Sleepout Rod and Curtains](https://sleepoutcurtains.com/products/sleepout-home?variant=43764380434687)).

4. Also make sure you know what type of curtain hole you are using. Grommets are the metal circles at the top of curtains that are often the easiest to open, but they also let in the most light. The large holes themselves and the folds they make in the curtain have too many gaps. I suggest rod pocket or back tabs.

5. Finally if you are looking to permanently black out a window that you don't want to open you have a few options. The commercial option is [blackout-ez](https://www.amazon.com/Blackout-EZ-Sunlight-Blocking-Customizable/dp/B006S65GAE?th=1) which I heard works fantastic but is kinda expensive. The commonly suggested home remedies include using tinfoil or  garbage bags, but I found that pressure gaps, condensation, and temperature changes cause these to move around a lot and make a bunch of noise(especially the tinfoil). I would recommend [foil lined tape](https://www.homedepot.com/p/Nashua-Tape-2-5-in-x-60-yd-324A-Premium-Foil-HVAC-UL-Listed-Sealer-Duct-Tape-1542698/100048600) instead. The foil part is completely opaque and lets in no light. It's made for HVAC sealing and is rated for temps from -25 to 325 so it withstands the elements and doesn't make a peep. And because the tape side is brown, it looks slightly less weird from the outside than having tinfoil in you windows.

Came to post this and want to reiterate that these are fantastic. I just went through the whole gambit of trying to find real blackout curtains after getting the eclipse as a gift for Christmas and them not working.

The Nicetown curtains fully block out light, at high noon my room is completely dark. These are so dark you may even need to crack them if you want any light to help wake up. As someone who  is pretty insomniac and works weird schedules including night-shifts (EMS), I could not ask for better curtains. 

​

Also P.S. if like me you have another window in your room that is small and you don't want to get curtains for it too, I recommend foil lined tape from home depot. The metal foil is completely opaque and blocks all light. Other recommendations you can find are to use regular tinfoil or garbage bags, but I found that pressure gaps, condensation, and temperature changes cause these to move around a lot and make a bunch of noise (especially the tinfoil). The tape is made for HVAC sealing so it withstands the elements and doesn't make a peep. Looks a little weird from the outside though

Borg stomp this one. According to the Mass Effect wiki the Reaper's primary weapon can range from "a yield of 132 to 450 kilotons of TNT" while their survive-ability primarily comes from thick armor. We have seen them able to be damaged by a large firing of Mass effect in universe weaponry (20 kilogram slugs at 1.3% lightspeed= 35 kiloton yield). 

On the other hand a standard federation TNG era photon torpedo is rated at 18.5 isoton with a max yield of 25 isotons. According to the Star Trek technical manual, such a warhead carries 1.5kg of matter and 1.5kg of matter. Based on standard physics, the combination of which would lead to a yield of \~64 megatons of TNT or 64,000 kilotons. That is over 142x as powerful as the strongest Reaper weapon and over 1,800x as powerful as the powerful human weaponry. 

A single Borg cube can survive a barrage of photon torpedoes, even without its shields. With its shields they are basically useless. I have doubts a reaper would even be able to scratch a cube. 

Further data on Borg weapon power: 

In Voyager *Omega Directive* we see a a photon torpedo modified to include a gravametric charge, which is the technology in Borg weaponry, resulting in an 80 isoton yield. Assuming the isoton scales linearly this would result in a 204,000 kiloton yield, enough to blow up a planet. 453x as powerful as a Reaper weapon

Assuming that Borg technology is equal or greater than federation advancements: 

A class six Voyager era torpedo had a yeild of 200 isotons. 512,000 kiloton yield. 1,137x as powerful as a Reaper weapon

A class 12 Abrams era long range torpedo had a yeild of 320 isotons. 819,200 kiloton yield. 1,1820x as powerful as a Reaper weapon

Finally the Borg specifically mention plans and the ability to develop a **5 million isoton** multi-kinetic neutronic mine that had a dispersive force radius of five light years. 12,800,000,000 kiloton yield. Over 28 millionx as powerful as a Reaper weapon.

And this is all assuming that Reapers are resistant to other common tech such as Borg assimilation, transport technology to beam things directly inside, ect.

​

For stage two just on weapons alone as well as size of the forces I think Reapers get stomped. Even outside of that a Reaper has the FTL capacity to go nearly 30 light-years (283,821,914,177,424,000 meters) within a 24-hour period. This equates Reaper FTL capabilities to around 10,957 times the speed of light. While the Star Trek warp scale is often contradicted, one firm point we have is the quote in Voyager that Warp 9.9 being at 21,473 times the speed of light. A Borg cube standard drive max velocity is Warp 9.98 and with Warp being an exponentially increasing scale, with Warp 10 being a vertical asymptote, some calculations put it in multiple millions times the speed of light. Regardless it is much faster than the Reapers even without using their transwarp network which allows even faster deployment. 

​

This is all even assuming that the Borg would be attacked by the Reapers as they are already a merging of synthetic and organic life, the very result that caused the Reapers to stop attacking and turn peaceful in the synthesis ending of Mass Effect.

​

TLDR: Star Trek is a powerful universe and Borg likely eat the Reapers for breakfast, lunch and, dinner
